title: Postcolonial IR

cards.b: Mainstream IR was written mostly in the US and Britain, about the great powers. Postcolonial and Global IR ask: whose history counts? What if the world is seen from Delhi, Lagos or Lima? It is an emerging UPSC theme with links to Third World approaches.

Edward Said, Orientalism (1978): the West created the 'Orient' as backward, which justified rule. Frantz Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth (1961): colonialism wounds the mind, and decolonisation needs a new humanism. Gayatri Spivak, 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988): elites speak for the powerless. Homi Bhabha: hybridity and mimicry.

Textbook IR starts with the 1648 Westphalia peace, as if states began in Europe. Critics note that sovereignty was unequal: colonies lacked it, and 'standards of civilisation' decided who was a full state. John Hobson, The Eurocentric Conception of World Politics (2012) shows how racial hierarchy shaped Western IR. The Berlin Conference (1884-85) divided Africa without Africans. Racism is thus a hidden structure of international order.

Acharya and Buzan, 'Why is there no non-Western IR theory?' (2007), found rich ideas that had not been theorised: Kautilya's mandala, Chinese tianxia and 'harmony', Islamic and African traditions. Amitav Acharya's Global IR (ISA address, 2014) asks for a discipline grounded in world history, diverse theories and regional worlds, instead of replacing the West with the rest.

Mohammed Ayoob's subaltern realism (1995) says that for the Third World, state-making and internal security come first, unlike the North's external focus. Dependency and world-systems ideas (Prebisch, Frank, Wallerstein) and TWAIL (Third World Approaches to International Law) argue that international law serves imperial interest. Bandung 1955 and the NAM, NIEO appear as Southern agency.

• Realists: power politics is universal, not Western.
  • Risk of replacing one essentialism ('the West') with another.
  • Elites in the Global South can also be Eurocentric; the Third World is not one voice.
  • Obscure language; weak policy guidance.
  • Defenders: it exposes silent assumptions and widens the field.

Compare: Marxism (class and capital; postcolonialism adds race and culture), constructivism (ideas matter; postcolonialism asks whose ideas), feminism (gender; shares critique of the 'universal' subject). It also links with decolonial thought from Latin America (Quijano, Mignolo).

Edward Said's Culture and Imperialism (1993) and Homi Bhabha's The Location of Culture (1994) give the textual tools that postcolonial IR borrows.

Dipesh Chakrabarty's Provincializing Europe (2000) asks how Europe's history came to stand as universal history for everyone.

Nehru's anti-colonial IR, NAM, India's stance on Palestine, apartheid, and NIEO, and demands for a reformed UNSC all carry postcolonial concerns. India's civilisational ideas (Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, Panchsheel, Kautilya) feed Global IR. Scholars: Ranajit Guha, Dipesh Chakrabarty (Provincializing Europe, 2000), and Kanti Bajpai. Remember to note the risks of using civilisational pride to cover national interest.

Structure: problem, thinkers, Eurocentrism, Global IR, Third World security, critique, India.

Amitav Acharya's 2014 article 'Global IR and Regional Worlds' makes the case for a plural IR that recognises regional and non-Western theories.

Sanjay Seth's Postcolonial Theory and International Relations (2013) argues that the discipline still carries colonial assumptions.
